title: Education Running Out of Time Brad Littlejohn
author: Littlejohn, Brad
summary: Brad Littlejohn observes that our civilization's fear of wasted time — hyperactive schedules, phone dependence during waits, inability to watch a sunset — reflects a deeper loss of patience as a virtue. 'Patience' derives from the Latin for 'to suffer,' pointing to an ancient understanding that waiting is inherently difficult. Yet patience is the foundation of all genuine skill: Sullenberger had 19,000 hours of flight time; research shows approximately 10,000 hours to expertise across most disciplines. Applied to education, this law is stubbornly inviolable, yet decades of EdTech (iPads, Chromebooks, now AI tutors) have failed to shortcut it, with American test scores deteriorating throughout. Students using ChatGPT for term papers have 'few illusions that they are learning in the process' — many have arrived at nihilism: with machines ahead of them, gaining competence is pointless. Philosopher Byung-Chul Han describes this as 'directionless whizzing' — speed without destination. Excerpt from Littlejohn's forthcoming book: Left to Our Own Devices: Reclaiming Human Agency in the Age of the Machine.
points: 'Patience' derives from the Latin for 'to suffer' — the capacity for bearing time's passage is a virtue that pleasure-seeking has steadily eroded.
Elite performance requires irreducible time investment: Sullenberger had 19,000 hours; ~10,000 hours to expertise across most disciplines; this law does not bend for technology.
Classical education is a discipline, not a technique — parents expected 'rigor' without added time; the irreducible practices (reading, memorizing, writing, debating, repeating) cannot be shortcut.
AI tutors present the same problem as all prior EdTech: no one has explained how a technology designed to minimize effort suits a domain whose purpose is very nearly the opposite.
Students using AI for term papers have few illusions they are learning — many have arrived at nihilism: with machines ahead of them, gaining competence is pointless.
quotes: In some measure, this fear of waiting has always been part of our restless human natures, so much so that our word for bearing up under the burden of time — 'patience' — comes from the Latin word meaning 'to suffer'; and indeed 'longsuffering' is an archaic English synonym for the same virtue. To wait is to suffer, and in our age of pleasure-seeking, we have increasingly lost the capacity to suffer well.

Chesley Sullenberger III, who in 2009 became a national hero for successfully landing a passenger plane on the Hudson River without a single fatality, had by that point logged 19,000 hours, giving him the tacit knowledge to exercise flawless snap judgment under enormous pressure.

But the larger issue, I soon realized, was that parents came in thinking that classical education was a technique rather than a discipline, that it represented some kind of clever educational innovation that would allow students to progress faster and farther without any added time and effort.
No one has been yet been able to explain how a technology that is precisely designed to minimize effort and maximize output should be suitable for a domain whose purpose is very nearly the opposite.

The student, after all, who uses ChatGPT to research and write their term paper surely has few illusions that they are somehow learning in the process. Many of our young people seem to have emerged at a nihilistic conclusion: what is the point in gaining competence? The machines are there ahead of us already, or soon will be.

We are thus condemned to a 'directionless whizzing' — passively carried too and fro by forces or agents beyond our control or concern, like the blob-humans in WALL-E, forever being shuttled pointlessly around their spaceship.
